h2.text: The system must record it, and a notification must go out.

h4.text: This design has two goals: run on Azure without managing servers,

h5.text: and stay correct when requests overlap or services fail.

i4.text: Nginx and Let's Encrypt were the original plan, but Container Apps already handles HTTPS and routing, so they disappear.

i5.text: Authorization stays: the API still validates Auth0 tokens and checks permissions.

i6.text: The cost: relying on Azure's features and limits.

a1.text: Behind ingress: a Rust API and a notification worker, both container images.

a2.text: Azure starts, restarts, routes and scales them:

a3.text: the API by HTTP demand, Notifications by queue backlog.

a4.text: Functions could also work, with a different execution model; this keeps an ordinary Axum server.

a6.text: It even absorbed the switch from Python to Rust.

a7.text: The cost: you still maintain images and scaling rules, and scaling from zero can delay the first request.

o1.text: Now the hard part: update the database, then message the queue.

o2.text: Crash in between, and the return exists but the notification is lost.

o3.text: Reverse them, and a notification can go out for a failed update.

o4.text: So the outbox saves the change and the notification request in one PostgreSQL transaction.

o6.text: Loans keep working through a queue outage.

o7.text: The cost: extra processing, storage, and eventual delivery.

p1.text: The application decides what succeeds together, through a small interface: a transaction port.

p2.text: Lock, apply the rule, save, commit.

p4.text: That keeps rules testable with fake adapters, at the cost of more interfaces and wiring.

p6.text: But fakes can't prove real concurrency, so integration tests stay necessary.

b1.text: PostgreSQL won't publish that record by itself.

b2.text: So a scheduled Container Apps Job wakes, claims a bounded batch, publishes, records success, and exits.

b3.text: It runs even when the API has scaled to zero.

b4.text: The one-minute schedule adds delay, and runs even with no work.

v1.text: Service Bus buffers the request, so Loan and Notifications needn't be up at the same time.

v2.text: Every responsibility gets a managed home.

v3.text: PostgreSQL for loan state. Cosmos DB for notification jobs.

v4.text: A registry for images. Identities and Key Vault for access.

v5.text: Monitor for failures. Storage for Terraform state.

v7.text: Each adds cost or complexity, and Cosmos was a choice, not a necessity.

d2.text: Service Bus accepts a message, the publisher crashes before recording that, then retries.

d4.text: A stable event ID lets Notifications check the existing job instead of blindly sending again.

l1.text: And two workers could still hold copies at once.

l2.text: A lease records temporary ownership: this job, this owner, until this time.

l4.text: If worker A crashes, ownership expires, and another worker can recover.

l6.text: The lease says who may process; Cosmos ETags enforce it, applying a change only if the record is unchanged since it was read.

l7.text: The cost: expiry, renewal and ownership checks must be right.

r6.text: Malformed or repeatedly failing? Dead-letter it for investigation.

r7.text: One window stays open: the provider accepts the email, then the worker crashes before recording success.

r8.text: So the design must not promise exactly-once email.

c1.text: These mechanisms improve failure handling, and they add complexity.

c2.text: Not every choice was required, or the simplest.

c3.text: Their value is being able to explain and demonstrate the failure each one addresses.
